indicators.question: Effective sector analysis and planning capacity: Is there a functioning capacity to undertake useful sector analysis of existing and emerging infrastructure gaps and service delivery shortfalls to inform national and sector strategic planning and prioritization?
indicators.incipient: Sector analysis results are rarely used in the following functions and then only in a few sectors: (i) formulating national and sector priorities and strategies; (ii) screening projects' project documents entering into the preparation and appraisal pipeline; (iii) estimating economic benefits from sector projects; and (iv) selecting projects and programs for inclusion in the medium-term and annual budgets.
indicators.nascent: Sector analysis results are used in at least two of the following functions in some sectors: (i) formulating national and sector priorities and strategies; (ii) screening projects' project documents entering into the preparation and appraisal pipeline; (iii) estimating economic benefits from sector projects; and (iv) selecting projects and programs for inclusion in the medium-term and annual budgets.
indicators.emerging: Sector analysis results are effectively used in at least three of the following functions in some sectors: (i) formulating national and sector priorities and strategies; (ii) screening projects' project documents entering into the preparation and appraisal pipeline; (iii) estimating economic benefits from sector projects; and (iv) selecting projects and programs for inclusion in the medium-term and annual budgets.
indicators.advanced: Sector analysis results are effectively used in all of the following functions in most sectors: (i) formulating national and sector priorities and strategies; (ii) screening projects' project documents entering into the preparation and appraisal pipeline; (iii) estimating economic benefits from sector projects; and (iv) selecting projects and programs for inclusion in the medium-term and annual budgets in line with sector priorities.

indicators.question: Strategic guidance for project identification and prioritization: Does the government publish authoritative national and sector strategic investment plans that can be used to guide project identification and subsequent prioritization?
indicators.incipient: No national public investment strategy (or equivalent) has been developed.
indicators.nascent: A national public investment strategy (or equivalent) has been developed, but with only loose attention to fiscal constraints and limited costing and performance feedback from projects under implementation or operation.
indicators.emerging: A national public investment strategy (or equivalent) has been developed, which is part of or aligned with the national development strategy/plan, is constrained by a fiscal framework and incorporates useful, but ad hoc, costing and performance feedback from projects under implementation and operation.
indicators.advanced: A national public investment strategy (or equivalent) has been developed, which is part of or aligned with the national development strategy/plan, is constrained by a realistic fiscal framework and systematically incorporates costing and performance feedback from projects under implementation and operation.

indicators.question: Screening based on project concept note (project profile): Is there a standardized process for developing informative project concept notes (project profiles) for screening projects based on strategic relevance, rationale (project logic and demand for project services) and impediments to success?
indicators.incipient: There is no standardized process for developing and submitting project concept notes for review.
indicators.nascent: Project sponsors from the main infrastructure sectors submit project concept notes for central agency/line ministry review, but these are not always fully specified.
indicators.emerging: Most project sponsors submit project concept notes for central agency/line ministry review, but these are not always fully specified.
indicators.advanced: All project sponsors submit fully specified project concept notes, covering strategic relevance, rationale (logic and demand) and impediments to success, for central agency/line ministry review.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of preliminary project screening: Does preliminary screening, based on review of a project concept note (project profile), result in rejection of non-strategic projects, projects where the rationale is weak, or projects likely to face insurmountable impediments to success?
indicators.incipient: Few, if any, projects are rejected or required to be revised based on central agency/line ministry (LM) review.
indicators.nascent: More than 5% of project concept notes (project profiles) in most project categories are rejected or required to be revised based on central agency/LM review.
indicators.emerging: More than 10% of project concept notes (project profiles) in most project categories are rejected or required to be revised based on central agency/LM review.
indicators.advanced: More than 15% of project concept notes (project profiles) in most project categories are rejected or required to be revised based on central agency/LM review.

en.name: Appraisal and value for public money

indicators.question: Robust project appraisal procedures: Do formal procedures for project appraisal exist, with clear delineation of scope, responsibilities for appraisal activities, and decision-making powers?
indicators.incipient: The scope of project appraisal requirements, the roles and responsibilities for project appraisal and decision-making powers are not defined.
indicators.nascent: The scope of project appraisal requirements, the roles and responsibilities for project appraisal or decision-making powers are weakly defined within individual line ministries and agencies, between line ministries and central agencies, and within and between different central agencies.
indicators.emerging: The scope of project appraisal requirements, the roles and responsibilities for project appraisal or decision-making powers are not fully defined within individual line ministries and agencies, between line ministries and central agencies, and within and between different central agencies.
indicators.advanced: The scope, size and nature of project appraisal requirements, the roles and responsibilities for project appraisal and the decision-making powers are clear within individual line ministries and agencies, between line ministries and central agencies, and within and between different central agencies.

indicators.question: Standardized project appraisal guidelines and methodologies: Are there standardized guidelines and technical methodologies for performing project appraisal, which make social cost-benefit analysis the default method for determining value for public money, are differentiated by sector and supported by national parameter values for consistent application?
indicators.incipient: There are no standardized national guidelines or methodologies for project appraisal.
indicators.nascent: Standardized national guidelines for performing project appraisal exist, but are not yet detailed enough to support consistent application across projects.
indicators.emerging: Standardized national guidelines and technical methodologies for performing project appraisal exist and make social cost-benefit analysis the default method for determining value for public money, but are not differentiated by sector or are not supported by comprehensive national parameter values for consistent application.
indicators.advanced: Standardized national guidelines and technical methodologies for performing project appraisal exist, make social cost-benefit analysis the default method for determining value for public money, are differentiated by main sector and supported by comprehensive national parameter values for consistent application.

indicators.question: Comprehensive appraisal: In addition to value for public money, does appraisal take account of risks (to implementation and to benefit realization) and their management, of project deliverability, and of social, environmental and financial sustainability?
indicators.incipient: There is no provision for comprehensive appraisal.
indicators.nascent: Project appraisal includes only a basic risk analysis and is lacking in one or more areas of: i) assessment of project deliverability; ii) social and environmental impact assessment; iii) or financial and budgetary sustainability analysis.
indicators.emerging: Project appraisal includes adequate risk analysis, but is weak in one or more areas of: i) risk management; ii) assessment of project deliverability; iii) social and environmental impact assessment; iv) or financial and budgetary sustainability analysis.
indicators.advanced: Project appraisal includes full-scope analysis and management of risk, assessment of project deliverability, social and environmental impact assessment and financial and budgetary sustainability analysis.

indicators.question: Realistic lifecycle cost estimation: Does appraisal include estimation of project life-cycle costs (capital and O&M) based on up-to-date and reliable market-based unit cost data, and including evidence-based allowances for cost overruns?
indicators.incipient: Only capital costs are estimated in any detail, using regulated unit costs that do not reflect recent market experience and there is no allowance for cost overruns.
indicators.nascent: Life-cycle costs are estimated using regulated unit costs that are infrequently updated to reflect market experience and cost overruns are only allowed for through the application of an arbitrary contingency factor.
indicators.emerging: Life-cycle costs are estimated using market-based unit costs, but the reliability of such data is uncertain, and cost overruns are only allowed for through the application of a contingency factor that is not project specific.
indicators.advanced: Life-cycle costs are estimated based on up-to-date and reliable market-based unit cost data and include allowances for cost overruns based on analysis of past performance of completed projects of a similar nature and size.

indicators.question: Access to specialist project appraisal capacities: Do project sponsors have access to the specialist expertise necessary to carry out project appraisal or have the in-house capacity to act as an 'intelligent client' where project appraisal activities are outsourced?
indicators.incipient: National appraisal capacities are close to non-existent, either in-house or externally.
indicators.nascent: Project sponsors have great difficulty accessing the specialist expertise necessary to carry out project appraisal, either in-house or externally, or are very short of the in-house capacity to act as an 'intelligent client' where project appraisal activities are outsourced.
indicators.emerging: Project sponsors cannot always access the specialist expertise necessary to carry out project appraisal, either in-house or externally, or are short of the in-house capacity to act as an 'intelligent client' where project appraisal activities are outsourced.
indicators.advanced: Project sponsors have access to the specialist expertise necessary to carry out project appraisal and/or the in-house capacity to act as an 'intelligent client' where project appraisal activities are outsourced.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of discipline in confirming public value for money: What % share of non-minor, non-donor projects is subject to social cost-benefit analysis (or cost-effectiveness analysis where more appropriate) as part of project appraisal?
indicators.incipient: Social cost-benefit analysis is not performed as part of project appraisal.
indicators.nascent: More than 25% of non-minor, non-donor projects are subject to social cost-benefit analysis (or cost-effectiveness analysis where more appropriate) as part of project appraisal.
indicators.emerging: More than 50% of non-minor, non-donor projects are subject to social cost-benefit analysis (or cost-effectiveness analysis where more appropriate) as part of project appraisal.
indicators.advanced: More than 90% of non-minor, non-donor projects are subject to social cost-benefit analysis (or cost-effectiveness analysis where more appropriate) as part of project appraisal.

indicators.question: Robust procedures for independent review of project appraisal: Do formal procedures for independent review exist, with clear delineation of scope, responsibilities and linkages with decision making?
indicators.incipient: There is minimal or no independent technical review of appraisals, or the conduct of prefeasibility appraisals, by an entity independent of the project sponsoring agency/ministry and no external entity has sufficient technical expertise to conduct a credible technical review.
indicators.nascent: Procedures are in place that require major projects to be subjected to technical review by an entity that is independent of the project sponsoring agency/ministry, but has limited expertise in the conduct of project appraisal.
indicators.emerging: Procedures are in place that require non-minor projects to be subjected to technical review or prefeasibility appraisals by an entity that is independent of the project sponsoring agency/ministry and has a reasonable level of expertise in the conduct of project appraisal.
indicators.advanced: Procedures are in place that require all appraisals of non-minor, high risk or novel projects to be subjected to technical review or independent prefeasibility by an entity independent of the project sponsoring agency/ministry and with a high level of expertise in the conduct of project appraisal.

indicators.question: Comprehensive coverage of independent review: Does independent review cover all of the following: i) the quality of application of appraisal guidelines and methodologies; ii) realism of lifecycle cost estimates; iii) the realism of the assumptions behind the appraisal; and iv) soundness of the appraisal findings?
indicators.incipient: Independent review meets none of the content requirements.
indicators.nascent: Independent review only covers the quality of application of appraisal guidelines and national appraisal methodology.
indicators.emerging: Independent review covers i) the quality of application of appraisal guidelines and methodologies, and ii) realism of lifecycle cost estimates, but pays little attention to the realism of the assumptions behind the appraisal and the soundness of the appraisal findings.
indicators.advanced: Independent review if[JC1]  comprehensive, covering: i) the quality of application of appraisal guidelines and methodologies; ii) realism of lifecycle cost estimates; iii) the realism of the assumptions behind the appraisal; and iv) soundness of the appraisal findings.

indicators.question: Quantitative performance in applying independent review procedures: What % share of non-minor projects is subject to comprehensive independent review by reviewers with no connection to the project sponsor?
indicators.incipient: Few, if any, non-minor projects are subject to independent review.
indicators.nascent: 25% or more of non-minor projects are subject to independent review.
indicators.emerging: 50% or more of non-minor projects are subject to independent review.
indicators.advanced: 100% of non-minor projects are subject to independent review.

indicators.question: Robust procedures for selecting projects for budget funding: Does budget preparation include formal procedures and criteria for selecting new projects for funding, including verification of positive appraisal, availability of fiscal space and contribution to achieving strategic investment priorities?
indicators.incipient: There are no formal procedures or defined criteria for selecting new projects for funding, and projects enter the budget largely in a non-transparent way.
indicators.nascent: Procedures exist, but are too weak to control emergency or politically motivated projects, and selection criteria are either weak, unclear or incomplete, so that selection decisions may lack transparency.
indicators.emerging: Formal procedures exist, but are lax with respect to emergency and politically motivated projects, and selection criteria exist but are either incomplete or not fully defined, leaving some room for some lack of transparency in selection decisions.
indicators.advanced: There are robust formal procedures, which apply to all projects, and well-defined criteria for selecting new projects for funding, including verification of positive appraisal findings, availability of fiscal space and contribution to achieving strategic investment priorities.

indicators.question: Annual budgeting informed by multi-year perspective of capital expenditure: Are reliable forward estimates prepared for the capital budget to inform the government and parliament of the future budgetary implications of their current decisions?
indicators.incipient: There are no forward estimates of the expenditure implications of multi-year projects.
indicators.nascent: Multi-year estimates of the forward expenditure implications of ongoing projects are prepared for budgetary purposes, but these are often not complete or reliable.
indicators.emerging: Multi-year estimates are prepared for the capital budget, broken down between expenditure on baseline and new projects, but the figures are not comprehensive or reliable.
indicators.advanced: Comprehensive and reliable multi-year estimates are prepared for the capital budget, broken down between expenditure on baseline and new projects, to provide information on the future budgetary implications of current decisions.

indicators.question: Transparent and comprehensive capital budget: Is the budget comprehensive in its coverage of capital expenditure, including donor projects, and transparent in identifying the total cost of individual multi-year projects?
indicators.incipient: There is significant extra-budgetary capital expenditure and only the annual cost of projects is included in the budget.
indicators.nascent: The capital budget is reasonably comprehensive, including coverage of the most important donor projects, and the total cost of the most important multi-year projects is identified.
indicators.emerging: With some relatively minor exceptions, the budget is comprehensive in its coverage of capital expenditure, including coverage of most donor projects, and identifies the total cost of most individual multi-year projects.
indicators.advanced: The budget is fully comprehensive in its coverage of capital expenditure and identifies the total cost of all individual multi-year projects.

indicators.question: Full funding of ongoing projects: Is budget funding for performing ongoing projects assured before allocations are made to new projects?
indicators.incipient: Ongoing and new projects compete for budget funding on an equal footing during budget preparation.
indicators.nascent: Funding for ongoing projects is frequently lower than the efficient disbursement plan in order to make way for funding new projects.
indicators.emerging: Funding for ongoing projects is sometimes lower than the efficient disbursement plan in order to make way for funding new projects.
indicators.advanced: Funding for performing ongoing projects is never restricted to make way for new projects.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of capital budget execution: On average over the last three complete budget years, what is the % variance between the initially voted annual capital budget and the budget as disbursed?
indicators.incipient: In two or all of the last three years, the actual capital development or expenditure deviated from budgeted capital expenditure by an amount equivalent to more than [25%] of budgeted capital spending.
indicators.nascent: In no more than one out of the last three years has the actual development or capital expenditure deviated from budgeted capital expenditure by an amount equivalent to more than [25%] of budgeted capital spending.
indicators.emerging: In no more than one out of the last three years has the actual development or capital expenditure deviated from budgeted capital expenditure by an amount equivalent to more than [20%] of budgeted capital spending.
indicators.advanced: In no more than one out of the last three years has the actual development or capital expenditure deviated from budgeted capital expenditure by an amount equivalent to more than [15%] of budgeted capital spending.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator in assuring adequacy of funding for ongoing projects: On average over the last three complete budget years, what has been the % ratio of the annual capital budget to the total balance to complete the ongoing project portfolio?

Quantitative effectiveness indicator of inter-ministry variability in capital budget execution: On average over the last three complete budget years, what has been the variance in the composition of capital spending across agencies compared to the overall variance in capital spending (D4.Q1)?
indicators.incipient: In two or all of the last three years, the variance in the composition of capital spending across agencies exceeded the overall deviation in capital expenditure by more than [25] percentage points.
indicators.nascent: In no more than one out of the last three years has the variance in the composition of capital spending across agencies exceeded the overall deviation in capital spending by more than [25] percentage points.
indicators.emerging: In no more than one out of the last three years has the variance in the composition of capital spending across agencies exceeded the overall deviation in capital spending by more than [20] percentage points.
indicators.advanced: In no more than one out of the last three years has the variance in the composition of capital spending across agencies exceeded the overall deviation in capital spending by more than [15] percentage points.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator in controlling arrears: On average over the last three complete budget years, what is the size of capital expenditure arrears as a % share of the annual capital budget?
indicators.incipient: The stock of arrears exceeds 10% of total capital expenditure.
indicators.nascent: The stock of arrears constitutes 2%-10% of total capital expenditure; and there is no evidence that it has been reduced significantly in the last two years.
indicators.emerging: The stock of arrears for capital spending is below 2% of total capital expenditure, but is growing faster than the real economic growth rate over the past two years, or is in the range 2%-10% of total capital expenditure and there is evidence that it has been reduced significantly (i.e. more than 25%) in the last two years.
indicators.advanced: The stock of arrears for capital spending is low (i.e. below 2% of total capital expenditure) and growing no faster than the real economic growth rate over the past two years.

indicators.question: Robust legal and regulatory framework that supports transparency and competitiveness: Is the legal and regulatory framework for procurement of capital projects and associated consultancy services fully specified at all levels - primary legislation and supporting lower-level legislation/regulations - and aimed at ensuring economy, fairness, transparency, proportionality and integrity?
indicators.incipient: Primary legislation for procurement is missing or poorly developed and does not provide a satisfactory basis for transparent and competitive procurement.
indicators.nascent: The legal and regulatory framework for procurement includes primary legislation, but is only partially developed in other respects with the consequence that it is difficult to ensure that the principles of economy, fairness, transparency, proportionality and integrity will be achieved.
indicators.emerging: The legal and regulatory framework for procurement is developed in most respects, including primary legislation, but with some gaps, and, although designed to achieve economy, fairness, transparency, proportionality and integrity, it may not always support the achievement of these principles in all their dimensions.
indicators.advanced: The legal and regulatory framework for procurement is fully developed in all respects and is designed to achieve economy, fairness, transparency, proportionality and integrity.

indicators.question: Competitive procurement methods: Does the established procurement system prioritize - de jure and de facto - the use of the most competitive procurement methods, while specifying less competitive methods and setting out clear conditions for their use?
indicators.incipient: Non-competitive procurement is used with no practical restrictions.
indicators.nascent: While competitive procurement methods are favored, there are few practical restrictions on the use of non-competitive methods which are used regularly.
indicators.emerging: The procurement system prioritizes the use of competitive procurement methods on paper, but there are some departures in practice because of weaknesses in discipline or loose specification of the conditions for using less competitive methods.
indicators.advanced: The procurement system prioritizes the use of the most competitive procurement methods, both on paper and in practice, while also setting out strict conditions for the use of properly defined, less competitive methods.

indicators.question: Fair and timely procurement complaints process: Does the procurement complaints process adequately balance the rights of complainants, including an independent appeals mechanism, against system efficiency, and does it deliver findings within timeframes that do not disrupt procurement or deter complaints?
indicators.incipient: The complaints process either does not exist or is ineffective to the point where it might as well not exist.
indicators.nascent: A complaints process exists, but takes a long time, may deliver unreliable findings or has undue restrictions on the right of appeal.
indicators.emerging: The procurement complaints process is generally fair and timely, but delays sometimes occur, legitimate complaints are sometimes turned away or the appeals mechanism does not always function properly.
indicators.advanced: The procurement complaints process adequately balances the rights of complainants, including an independent appeals mechanism, against system efficiency, and delivers findings within timeframes that do not disrupt procurement or deter complaints.

indicators.question: Systematic collection and analysis of procurement data: Is there a system for collecting reliable data on the entire procurement process that is used for analysis of trends, levels of participation, efficiency and economy of procurement, and compliance with requirements?
indicators.incipient: There is no system for collecting data on the procurement process.
indicators.nascent: There is a rudimentary system for collecting data on the procurement process, but the data is partial or unreliable, significantly restricting the scope or quality of analysis.
indicators.emerging: There is a system for collecting data on the procurement process, but it does not cover the entire process or has some issues with data reliability, impairing the range or quality of the analysis.
indicators.advanced: There is a well-developed system for collecting reliable data on the entire procurement process that is used for analysis of trends, levels of participation, efficiency and economy of procurement and compliance with requirements.

indicators.question: Proper procurement planning: Is procurement planned properly, with procurement plans prepared sufficiently in advance and in adequate detail to inform budgeting and cash management processes and to support smooth project implementation?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful procurement planning for infrastructure projects.
indicators.nascent: There is some rudimentary procurement planning, but it is not carried out consistently and is poorly coordinated with budgeting.
indicators.emerging: Procurement planning is carried out at appraisal and subsequently updated, but updating is not sufficiently regular and there are some gaps in coordination with budgeting.
indicators.advanced: Procurement is planned well in advance, beginning with a preliminary procurement plan that is prepared at appraisal, and which is then regularly updated and enhanced during detailed project preparation so that it feeds directly into the budget preparation and execution process.

indicators.question: Robust contract administration management: Are roles and responsibilities for contract management well defined, conditions for contract amendment established, and an enforceable dispute resolution mechanism in place?
indicators.incipient: Arrangements for contract administration management either do not exist, or are ineffective to the point where they might as well not exist.
indicators.nascent: Roles and responsibilities for contract management are loosely defined, conditions for contract amendment are weakly specified or resolution of disputes is problematic.
indicators.emerging: Roles and responsibilities for contract management are reasonably clear, but conditions for contract amendment are not fully specified or resolution of disputes is not always straightforward.
indicators.advanced: There are well-defined roles and responsibilities for contract management, together with established conditions for contract amendment and an enforceable dispute resolution mechanism.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of use of competitive procurement: Among all procured projects over the last 3 years, what % proportion of projects has been procured by an open and competitive bidding process involving 3 or more qualifying bids?
indicators.incipient: <50% number of projects.
indicators.nascent: 50%-75% number of projects.
indicators.emerging: 75%-95% number of projects.
indicators.advanced: >95% number of projects.

indicators.question: Standardized project management process: Are there standardized project management arrangements in place, involving defined roles and responsibilities, appropriate delegation, and a consistent approach to implementation planning?
indicators.incipient: In practical terms, there are no standardized project management arrangements.
indicators.nascent: Standardized project management arrangements exist, but are quite general with respect to responsibilities, delegations or implementation planning and may not be uniformly applied.
indicators.emerging: Standardized project management arrangements, with well-defined roles and responsibilities and a consistent approach to implementation planning, are in place, but may not be uniformly applied and include some inefficiencies in the delegation of responsibility for decision making.
indicators.advanced: Standardized project management arrangements are in place and uniformly applied, with well-defined roles and responsibilities, appropriate delegation of responsibility for decision making to the level where it is best exercised, and a consistent approach to implementation planning.

indicators.question: Reporting and monitoring implementation progress: Is there timely and accurate reporting on project progress, both financial and physical, and responsive monitoring of reports, including active total project cost management?
indicators.incipient: There is no reporting on project progress or, if there is, it is a rudimentary administrative exercise only with no practical impact on the course of project implementation.
indicators.nascent: Basic reporting on project progress is performed but may be limited to financial progress only and timeliness, reliability and responsiveness to problems are very uneven.
indicators.emerging: Reporting on project progress, financial and physical, takes place and includes management of total project costs, but timeliness, reliability and responsiveness to problems are uneven.
indicators.advanced: Reporting on project progress, financial and physical, is both timely and accurate, results in punctual action being taken to resolve problems and includes active management of total project costs.

indicators.question: Process for adjusting projects: Is there clear authority for resolving issues relating to problem projects and for making in-year budget reallocations between projects progressing at different speeds?
indicators.incipient: There is no clearly defined process for adjusting projects, leading to either excessive rigidity or ad hoc adjustments.
indicators.nascent: Authorities for resolving issues relating to problem projects and for making in-year budget reallocations between projects progressing at different speeds are defined in general terms only, leaving them subject to interpretation, and often do not operate effectively, resulting in either unnecessary rigidity or too much flexibility.
indicators.emerging: Authorities for resolving issues relating to problem projects and for making in-year budget reallocations between projects progressing at different speeds are established, but do not always operate effectively.
indicators.advanced: Authorities for resolving issues relating to problem projects and for making in-year budget reallocations between projects progressing at different speeds are clearly defined and operate effectively.

indicators.question: Periodic portfolio rationalization: Are there guidelines in place for periodic rationalization of the portfolio of ongoing investment projects to reflect legacy projects, worsening macro-fiscal conditions, or event- or data-driven shifts in investment priorities?
indicators.incipient: There are no guidelines for portfolio rationalization and any rationalizations are very infrequent or arbitrary.
indicators.nascent: There are no standing guidelines for portfolio rationalization, but structured rationalizations with their own guidelines do take place from time to time, but the triggers for such rationalizations are not clear.
indicators.emerging: There are no standing guidelines for portfolio rationalization, but structured rationalizations with their own guidelines do take place from time to time and the triggers for such rationalizations are well defined.
indicators.advanced: Standing operational guidelines are in place for periodic rationalization of the portfolio of ongoing investment projects and are applied to reflect legacy projects, worsening macro-fiscal conditions, or event- or data-driven shifts in investment priorities.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of cost overruns: What is the weighted average inflation-adjusted cost overrun for non-minor projects completed in the last three years?
indicators.incipient: The three-year weighted average of the cost overruns is 30% or higher.
indicators.nascent: The three-year weighted average of the cost overruns is lower than 30%.
indicators.emerging: The three-year weighted average of the cost overruns is lower than 10%.
indicators.advanced: The three-year weighted average of the cost overruns is lower than 5%.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of time overruns: What is the weighted average time overrun for non-minor projects completed in the last three years?
indicators.incipient: The three-year weighted average of the time overruns is 100% or higher.
indicators.nascent: The three-year weighted average of the time overruns is lower than 100%.
indicators.emerging: The three-year weighted average of the time overruns is lower than 30%.
indicators.advanced: The three-year weighted average of the time overruns is lower than 15%.

indicators.question: Sustainable funding for operations and maintenance expenditure: Are regulatory procedures in place for ensuring adequate operations and maintenance funding of projects for proper service delivery?
indicators.incipient: There are no regulatory procedures for ensuring adequate funding for operations and maintenance, which, as a consequence, are systematically underfunded.
indicators.nascent: Basic regulatory procedures are in place for funding operations and maintenance expenditures - through user charges where applicable or the budget where not - but frequently do not function effectively in ensuring proper service delivery, either because of design weaknesses or political interference.
indicators.emerging: Regulatory procedures are in place for funding operations and maintenance expenditures - through user charges where applicable or the budget where not - but sometimes do not function effectively in ensuring proper service delivery, either because of design weaknesses or political interference.
indicators.advanced: Regulatory procedures are in place and functioning for ensuring adequate operations and maintenance funding - through user charges where applicable or the budget where not - for proper service delivery.

indicators.question: Management systems for operations and maintenance (O&M): Is there a process, with guidelines, for planning and tracking O&M expenditures and a system for monitoring impacts on service delivery?
indicators.incipient: Planning and tracking of O&M expenditures and monitoring their impacts on service delivery is not done in a systematic way.
indicators.nascent: There is a process, supported by clear guidelines, for planning O&M expenditures, but no tracking of such expenditures and no system for monitoring the impacts on service delivery.
indicators.emerging: There is a process, supported by clear guidelines, for planning and tracking O&M expenditures, but no system for monitoring the impacts on service delivery.
indicators.advanced: There is a process, supported by clear guidelines, for planning and tracking O&M expenditures and a system for monitoring the impacts on service delivery.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator in assuring adequate maintenance expenditure: What is the average percentage maintenance funding shortfall - needs compared with actual allocations - for selected major projects and/or a representative sector?
indicators.incipient: <50% of needs met.
indicators.nascent: 50-75% of needs met.
indicators.emerging: 75-95% of needs met.
indicators.advanced: >95% of needs met.

indicators.question: Project-level financial and performance audits: Are timely external financial and performance audits carried out for individual non-minor projects on completion?
indicators.incipient: Few, if any, external financial and performance audits are performed.
indicators.nascent: External financial audits are carried out for the majority (more than 50%) of individual non-minor projects on completion, but submitted with some delay (over 50% within a year of completion), and there are very few, if any, performance audits.
indicators.emerging: External financial audits are carried out for most (more than 75%) individual non-minor projects on completion and submitted in a reasonably timely fashion (over 75% within a year of completion), but external performance audits are.
indicators.advanced: External financial and performance audits are carried out for all individual non-minor projects on completion and submitted in a timely fashion (95% within a year of completion).

indicators.question: Completion review and ex post review process: Is there a formal system of mandatory project completion review and sampled-based ex post review, which is supported by guidelines and an established feedback mechanism?
indicators.incipient: There is no system for formal project completion review and ex post review.
indicators.nascent: There is a formal system of mandatory project completion review with supporting guidelines, but feedback to project design is unreliable and there is no system for ex post review.
indicators.emerging: There is a formal system of mandatory project completion review and sampled-based ex post review, but guidelines for ex post review are missing or not sufficiently detailed and the feedback to project design and strategic planning is not reliable.
indicators.advanced: There is a formal system of mandatory project completion review and sampled-based ex post review, which is supported by detailed guidelines and an established feedback mechanism.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator of carrying out completion reviews: What proportion of completed projects are subject to a formal completion review?
indicators.incipient: Less than 50% of projects are subject to a formal completion review.
indicators.nascent: More than 50% of projects are subject to a formal completion review.
indicators.emerging: More than 75% of projects are subject to a formal completion review.
indicators.advanced: All projects are subject to a formal completion review.

indicators.question: Quantitative effectiveness indicator in carrying out ex post reviews: What proportion of completed non-minor projects are subject to a formal ex post review involving examination of relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability?
indicators.incipient: Few, if any, completed projects are subject to ex post review.
indicators.nascent: At least 5% of completed non-minor projects and the majority (more than 50%) of mega projects are subject to a formal ex post review involving examination of relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability.
indicators.emerging: At least 10% of completed non-minor projects and most (more than 75%) of mega projects are subject to a formal ex post review involving examination of relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability.
indicators.advanced: At least 20% of completed non-minor projects and all mega projects are subject to a formal ex post review involving examination of relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact and sustainability.

indicators.question: Regulated scope and definition of PIM: Is public investment formally defined - in relation to economic nature, funding source and asset ownership - by law or regulation so that the scope of the public investment management system is fixed?
indicators.incipient: There is no definition of public investment in the legal framework.
indicators.nascent: There is a definition of public investment in the legal framework, but it is not specific enough, leaving many gray areas in the scope of the public investment management system.
indicators.emerging: Public investment is formally defined by law or regulation, but there are some ambiguities in relation to economic nature, funding source or asset ownership, which mean that scope of the public investment management system is sometimes subject to interpretation.
indicators.advanced: Public investment is formally defined - in relation to economic nature, funding source and asset ownership - by law or regulation so that the scope of the public investment management system is firmly fixed.

indicators.question: Hierarchical legal and regulatory framework for PIM: Is there a properly structured legal and regulatory framework for PIM, involving high-level legal authority and supporting regulations and detailed instructions?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful legal and regulatory framework for PIM.
indicators.nascent: The legal framework gives high-level authority for PIM, but detailed regulations, instructions and guidelines are incomplete.
indicators.emerging: The legal framework gives high-level authority for PIM and the supporting regulations are well developed, but instructions and guidelines for operationalization are incomplete or partially merged in regulations.
indicators.advanced: There is a structured legal and regulatory framework that gives high-level legal authority for PIM, is detailed in secondary legislation (or the equivalent) and is supported by implementable instructions and guidelines (or the equivalent).

indicators.question: Dedicated PIM body: Is there a designated body at the center of government - either under the finance ministry or planning ministry - that is responsible for coordinating and overseeing PIM and is accountable for system performance?
indicators.incipient: There is no functioning PIM unit, or the equivalent, at the center of government.
indicators.nascent: There is a designated body at the center of government that is responsible for coordinating and overseeing PIM, but its mandate is weak and there is no accountability for system performance.
indicators.emerging: There is a designated body at the center of government that is responsible for coordinating and overseeing PIM, but its mandate is not as strong as needed and accountability for system performance is diffused.
indicators.advanced: There is a designated body at the center of government with a strong mandate that is responsible for coordinating and overseeing PIM and is accountable for system performance.

indicators.question: Coordination of budgeting with PIM: Is there an active coordination mechanism between the body responsible for the budget and the body responsible for PIM so that they work together for overseeing eligibility for project funding, managing the ongoing project portfolio, and assuring adequate funding for O&M?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful coordination between budgeting and PIM.
indicators.nascent: There is ad hoc coordination of budgeting and PIM, which is more successful for new projects than it is for ongoing or completed projects, where there are significant weaknesses.
indicators.emerging: There is organized coordination of budgeting and PIM, which is more successful for new projects than it is for ongoing or completed projects, where there are some weaknesses.
indicators.advanced: There is an active coordination mechanism between the body responsible for the budget and the body responsible for PIM so that they work together for overseeing eligibility for project funding, managing the ongoing project portfolio, and assuring adequate funding for O&M.

indicators.question: Regulatory framework to control integrity risk: Is there a comprehensive regulatory and policy framework in place to control integrity risks throughout infrastructure development?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful regulatory and policy framework in place to control integrity risks.
indicators.nascent: Some basic elements of a policy framework for managing integrity risks exist, but operationalization and application to the specifics of infrastructure development are lagging.
indicators.emerging: A regulatory and policy framework is in place to control integrity risks, but is neither comprehensive nor sufficiently tailored to infrastructure development.
indicators.advanced: A comprehensive regulatory and policy framework is in place to comprehensively and sufficiently control integrity risks throughout infrastructure development.

indicators.question: Integrity risk assessment in project design: Does project preparation include integrity risk assessment and mitigation?
indicators.incipient: Integrity risk assessment and mitigation are not addressed in any meaningful way during project appraisal.
indicators.nascent: Integrity risk is addressed in an informal way only during project appraisal, but little attention is paid to mitigation.
indicators.emerging: An assessment of integrity risk is required as part of project appraisal, and mitigation and risk management measures are usually foreseen where risk is assessed as high.
indicators.advanced: A structured assessment of integrity risk is required as part of project appraisal, and mitigation and risk management measures must be specifically proposed where risk is assessed as high.

indicators.question: Integrity in implementation, procurement, and contract management: Does project implementation, procurement, and contract management follow principles of transparency and integrity?
indicators.incipient: Principles of transparency and integrity are not followed during implementation, procurement and contract management.
indicators.nascent: Some basic principles of transparency and integrity are followed during project implementation, procurement and contract management, but with significant departures from good practices.
indicators.emerging: Principles of transparency and integrity are followed during project implementation, procurement and contract management, but with some departures from good practices.
indicators.advanced: Recognized principles of transparency and integrity are strictly followed during project implementation, procurement and contract management.

indicators.question: Actions against breaches of integrity: Are breaches of integrity in infrastructure project development and implementation effectively investigated, prosecuted, and sanctioned?
indicators.incipient: There is no serious attempt to investigate breaches of integrity in infrastructure development and implementation.
indicators.nascent: Some breaches of integrity during infrastructure project development and implementation may be investigated, but there are frequent exceptions, and prosecution and sanctioning does not always follow.
indicators.emerging: Serious breaches of integrity during infrastructure project development and implementation are usually investigated, but prosecution and sanctioning is not systematic.
indicators.advanced: All breaches of integrity during infrastructure project development and implementation are effectively investigated, prosecuted, and sanctioned.

indicators.question: Transparency around project data: Are project data and information disclosed in a way that is easy to access, navigate, and analyze for accountability purposes and civil society monitoring?
indicators.incipient: Project data and information are not disclosed.
indicators.nascent: Project data and information are disclosed, but in an ad hoc way (on request, not automatic) and frequently in a form that is not easy to access, navigate, and analyze for accountability purposes and civil society monitoring.
indicators.emerging: Project data and information are disclosed, but not always in a form that is easy to access, navigate, and analyze for accountability purposes and civil society monitoring.
indicators.advanced: Project data and information are disclosed in a way that is easy to access, navigate, and analyze for accountability purposes and civil society monitoring.

indicators.question: Centralized PIM database across the project cycle: Is there one centralized PIM database for all public investment projects from conception to fruition?
indicators.incipient: There is no centralized PIM database.
indicators.nascent: There is a centralized PIM database for public investment projects, but it is not up to date or complete, and does not give full coverage of the project cycle.
indicators.emerging: There is a single centralized PIM database for public investment projects, but it is not always up to date or complete.
indicators.advanced: There is an up-to-date, single centralized PIM database for all public investment projects from conception to fruition.

indicators.question: Efficient data management and analysis: Is the PIM database automatized and computerized?
indicators.incipient: All data are paper based.
indicators.nascent: Spreadsheets are used to assemble and analyze paper submissions.
indicators.emerging: Basic PIM database is computerized, but the details and updates are not automated.
indicators.advanced: The PIM database is fully computerized and automated.

indicators.question: Information-led system performance improvements: Is the PIM database used for achieving efficiency gains through PIM workflows and processes - for example, performance monitoring and reporting?
indicators.incipient: Data analysis is not used for achieving PIM efficiency gains.
indicators.nascent: Basic analysis of spreadsheet data may be used to support PIM improvements, but reliability and coverage issues present limitations.
indicators.emerging: The PIM database is used in an ad hoc way for achieving efficiency gains through identification of better PIM workflows and processes.
indicators.advanced: The PIM database is used systematically for achieving efficiency gains through identification of better PIM workflows and processes.

indicators.question: Climate-smart public investment policy: Are public investment policies informed by climate change considerations and is the public investment strategy climate-informed?
indicators.incipient: Climate change is not taken into account in public investment policies, strategies or plans.
indicators.nascent: Public investment policies are informed by climate change considerations, but these considerations are not, or to a negligible extent, reflected in the public investment strategy/plan.
indicators.emerging: Public investment policies are informed by climate change considerations, and these considerations are partially reflected in the public investment strategy/plan.
indicators.advanced: Public investment policies are fully informed by climate change considerations, and these considerations are fully reflected in the public investment strategy/plan.

indicators.question: Climate-smart pre-screening: Are projects identified with climate change (CC) in mind and do project concept notes (project profiles) explicitly allow for climate change, distinguishing between CC-motivated projects and CC-affected/affecting projects?
indicators.incipient: No, or negligible, consideration is given to climate change in project concept notes.
indicators.nascent: Project concept notes are expected to give consideration to climate change, although this is implicit and the distinction between CC-motivated projects and CC-affected projects is not articulated.
indicators.emerging: Project concept notes are explicitly required to give consideration to climate change, but the different treatment of CC-motivated projects and CC-affected projects needs to be better articulated.
indicators.advanced: Project concept notes are explicitly required to give consideration to climate change and a clear distinction between the treatment of CC-motivated projects and CC-affected projects is made.

indicators.question: Climate-smart coordination within government: Is there an effective mechanism for coordinating investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation among the finance/planning ministry, environment ministry and sector ministries?
indicators.incipient: There is no mechanism for coordinating on climate change mitigation and adaptation investment among the finance/planning ministry, environment ministry and sector ministries.
indicators.nascent: There is a basic, but ad hoc, mechanism for coordinating on climate change mitigation and adaptation investment among the finance/planning ministry, environment ministry and sector ministries, but coordination is weak.
indicators.emerging: There is a formal mechanism for coordinating on climate change mitigation and adaptation investment among the finance/planning ministry, environment ministry and sector ministries, but there are some coordination gaps.
indicators.advanced: There is a formal mechanism which ensures effective coordination on climate change mitigation and adaptation investment among the finance/planning ministry, environment ministry and sector ministries.

indicators.question: Climate-smart coordination with private sector: Is there effective coordination of private sector engagement in climate-smart investment decision making?
indicators.incipient: There is no, or negligible, coordination of private sector engagement in climate-smart investment decision making.
indicators.nascent: There is some ad hoc coordination of private sector engagement in climate-smart investment decision making.
indicators.emerging: There is organized coordination of private sector engagement in climate-smart investment decision making, but it is not always effective.
indicators.advanced: Private sector engagement in climate-smart investment decision making is coordinated systematically and effectively.

indicators.question: Climate change risk assessment: Does appraisal involve an assessment of a project's climate change vulnerability and risk, followed by the design of adaptation options for high-risk projects?
indicators.incipient: There is no climate change vulnerability and risk assessment included as part of project appraisal.
indicators.nascent: Appraisal involves a qualitative assessment of a project's climate change vulnerability and risk, but it is not well structured and does not lead to the design of adaptation options for high-risk projects in a systematic way.
indicators.emerging: Appraisal involves a structured assessment of climate vulnerability and where relevant a climate and disaster risk assessment using available tools. Findings are recorded in project risk registers. Assessment leads to the design of adaptation options for high-risk projects, though not always systematically.
indicators.advanced: Appraisal involves a comprehensive assessment of a project's climate vulnerability and a structured climate and disaster risk assessment using the best available tools and updated climate projections. Risk registers comprehensively include climate risk. Assessment leads systematically to the design of adaptation options for high-risk projects.

indicators.question: Climate-smart appraisal guidelines: Is there formal methodological guidance on incorporating climate change in appraisal and on evaluating mitigation and adaptation actions and measures?
indicators.incipient: There is no methodological guidance on incorporating climate change in appraisal.
indicators.nascent: There is some high-level methodological guidance on incorporating climate change in appraisal, but it is not detailed enough to be operationalized consistently for the evaluation of mitigation and adaptation actions and measures.
indicators.emerging: There is formal methodological guidance on incorporating climate change in appraisal, but there are some gaps concerning methods for evaluating mitigation and adaptation actions and measures, which may lead to some inconsistencies in application.
indicators.advanced: There is formal, fully specified methodological guidance on incorporating climate change in appraisal, including methods for evaluating mitigation and adaptation actions and measures.

indicators.question: Value of greenhouse gas emissions and adaptation incorporated in appraisal methods: Are values for greenhouse gas emissions incorporated in SCBA, and is the choice of adaptation option optimized using SCBA?
indicators.incipient: Greenhouse gas emissions are neither quantified nor valued, and there is no serious analysis of adaptation options.
indicators.nascent: Greenhouse gas emissions are not quantified and valued in SCBA and adaptation options are chosen using a structured decision process (like multi-criteria analysis), but not SCBA.
indicators.emerging: Either values for greenhouse gas emissions are incorporated in SCBA or the choice of adaptation option is optimized using SCBA, but not both.
indicators.advanced: Nationally adopted values for greenhouse gas emissions are incorporated in SCBA and the choice of adaptation option is optimized using SCBA.

indicators.question: Climate-smart independent review: Does independent review cover consideration of the appraisal of mitigation and adaptation, including both the quality of the assessment and the robustness of the conclusions?
indicators.incipient: Independent review does not consider climate change aspects of a project.
indicators.nascent: Independent review covers climate change aspects of a project, but not in a systematic way.
indicators.emerging: Independent review considers the appraisal of mitigation or adaptation, but conducts weak assessment of the quality of the appraisal documents and the robustness of the conclusions.
indicators.advanced: Independent review considers the appraisal of mitigation and adaptation, including assessment of both the quality of the appraisal documents and the robustness of the conclusions.

indicators.question: Climate-smart budget tagging: Is investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation tagged for budgeting and reporting purposes and does analysis of tagged expenditure influence expenditure decisions?
indicators.incipient: Investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation actions and measures is not tagged in any meaningful way.
indicators.nascent: Investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation actions and measures is tagged for budgeting and reporting purposes, but tagging is not consistent and comprehensive, and analysis of tagged expenditure has limited influence on expenditure decisions.
indicators.emerging: Investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation actions and measures is tagged for budgeting and reporting purposes, and analysis of tagged expenditure has some influence on expenditure decisions, but tagging is not always consistent and comprehensive.
indicators.advanced: Investment in climate change mitigation and adaptation actions and measures is reliably tagged for budgeting and reporting purposes, and analysis of tagged expenditure has a direct influence on expenditure decisions.

indicators.question: Climate-smart selection and budgeting: Do actual budgetary decisions on investment projects take into account government-declared climate change priorities and the climate change risk to projects?
indicators.incipient: Budgetary decisions on investment projects take no account of the government's climate change policies or of climate change risks.
indicators.nascent: The government's climate change priorities or the climate change risk to projects are partially reflected in criteria for budgetary decisions, but in practice have a very limited impact on those decisions.
indicators.emerging: The government's climate change priorities and the climate change risk to projects are mostly reflected in criteria for budgetary decisions, but in practice have a limited impact on those decisions.
indicators.advanced: The government's climate change priorities and the climate change risk to projects are fully integrated into the criteria for budgetary decisions and impact on those decisions.

indicators.question: Climate-smart procurement standards: Is project procurement attuned to climate change mitigation and adaptation through the application of appropriate design standards and climate-smart project procurement practices?
indicators.incipient: Neither design standards nor project procurement practices take account of climate change in any meaningful way.
indicators.nascent: Climate-smart design standards or project procurement practices exist, but application during project procurement is very uneven.
indicators.emerging: Both climate-smart design standards and project procurement practices exist, but their application during project procurement is uneven.
indicators.advanced: Both climate-smart design standards and project procurement practices are consistently applied during project procurement.

indicators.question: Climate-smart implementation monitoring and adjustment: Does implementation monitoring include information on climate change risk that feeds into review and adjustment of project designs, as required?
indicators.incipient: Monitoring of implementation pays no, or negligible, attention to climate change.
indicators.nascent: Monitoring of implementation includes some requirements for information on emerging climate change risk, but these are not well specified and the feedback into adjustment of project designs is weak.
indicators.emerging: Monitoring of implementation includes requirements for information on emerging climate change risk, but these are not always well specified or fed into review and adjustment of project designs.
indicators.advanced: Monitoring of implementation includes requirements for specific information on emerging climate change risk, which then feeds directly into review and adjustment of project designs.

indicators.question: Climate-smart operations and maintenance: Are planning and funding of operational and maintenance expenditures consistent with sustainable delivery of project benefits in the face of emerging climate change risks?
indicators.incipient: Planning and funding of future operational and maintenance expenditure take no, or negligible, account of emerging climate change threats to sustainability.
indicators.nascent: Planning of future operational and maintenance expenditures takes some account of emerging climate change risks, but actual funding falls short of what is required for sustainable delivery of project benefits.
indicators.emerging: Planning of future operational and maintenance expenditures takes account of emerging climate change risks, but actual funding may not be fully compatible with sustainable delivery of project benefits.
indicators.advanced: Planning and funding of future operational and maintenance expenditures are fully consistent with sustainable delivery of project benefits in the face of emerging climate change risks.

indicators.question: Feedback to climate-smart project design: Do climate-informed project completion reports feed into consideration of climate change mitigation and adaptation in project design?
indicators.incipient: Project completion reports take no, or negligible, account of climate change.
indicators.nascent: There is some consideration of climate change in project completion reports, but it is not well structured, and findings are rarely reflected in mitigation and adaptation aspects of new project design.
indicators.emerging: Climate-informed project completion reports are prepared, but findings are not reflected systematically in mitigation and adaptation aspects of the design of new projects.
indicators.advanced: Findings from climate-informed project completion reports feed systematically into consideration of climate change mitigation and adaptation in the design of new projects.

indicators.question: Feedback to climate-smart public investment policy: Do climate-informed ex post impact assessments feed into the formulation of climate-smart public investment policy and into project identification and concept development?
indicators.incipient: Ex post impact assessments pay no, or negligible, attention to climate change.
indicators.nascent: A few ex post impact assessments are performed that take climate change into account, but the analysis is not well structured, and institutional weaknesses mean that findings are rarely reflected in climate-smart public investment policy and project identification and concept development.
indicators.emerging: Climate-informed ex post impact assessments are prepared, but findings are not reflected systematically in the formulation of climate-smart public investment policy and project identification and concept development.
indicators.advanced: Climate-informed ex post impact assessments feed systematically into the formulation of climate-smart public investment policy and project identification and concept development.

indicators.question: Whole-of-government policy for asset management: Are public asset management policy and objectives developed as a whole-of-government policy?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful whole-of-government public asset management policy.
indicators.nascent: There is a rudimentary public asset management policy which is intended to apply across the whole-of-government, but there are significant gaps in the content and coverage of the policy.
indicators.emerging: There is a public asset management policy which is intended to apply across the whole-of-government, but there are some gaps in the content and coverage of the policy in relation to linkages with project planning, PIM, budget management and service delivery.
indicators.advanced: There is a clearly defined, whole-of-government public asset management policy.

indicators.question: Plan for asset acquisition, O&M, and disposal: Is there an asset management plan in place for asset acquisition, O&M, and disposal?
indicators.incipient: There is no plan to guide public asset acquisition, O&M, and disposal.
indicators.nascent: There is a plan in place providing basic guidance on public asset acquisition, O&M, and disposal decisions, but it lacks detail and clarity in important areas, including linkage to project planning, PIM and budget management.
indicators.emerging: There is a plan in place providing guidance on public asset acquisition, O&M, and disposal decisions, but it lacks detail and clarity in some areas, including linkages to project planning, PIM and budget management.
indicators.advanced: There is a detailed plan in place providing clear guidance on public asset acquisition, O&M, and disposal decisions and linking to project planning, PIM and budget management.

indicators.question: Responsible organization(s): Is there an organization(s) responsible and accountable for asset registration and management, either internally to public bodies and/or externally?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful designation of responsibility for asset registration and management.
indicators.nascent: Organizational responsibility for asset registration and management is designated to relevant organization(s), but operationalization is not complete in important respects because of weak accountability arrangements.
indicators.emerging: Organizational responsibility and accountability for asset registration and management is designated to relevant organization(s), either internally to public bodies and/or externally, but operationalization is not complete because of some gray areas, especially with respect to accountability.
indicators.advanced: Organizational responsibility and accountability for asset registration and management is clearly designated to relevant organization(s), either internally to public bodies and/or externally.

indicators.question: Asset management capabilities: Does the responsible organization(s) for asset registration and management have the necessary competencies and skills to fulfil its functions properly?
indicators.incipient: Competencies and skills in asset registration are absent from relevant organizations.
indicators.nascent: The organization(s) responsible for asset registration and management have some of the necessary competencies and skills to fulfil their functions properly, but are lacking in important areas.
indicators.emerging: The organization(s) responsible for asset registration and management have most of the necessary competencies and skills to fulfil their functions properly but are lacking in certain areas.
indicators.advanced: The organization(s) responsible for asset registration and management have all the necessary competencies and skills to fulfil their functions properly.

indicators.question: Asset register: Is there a unitary and complete asset register linking to long-term financing needs and service delivery?
indicators.incipient: There is no unitary asset register.
indicators.nascent: There is a unitary asset register, but it is incomplete in important respects and the link to long-term financing needs and service delivery is missing.
indicators.emerging: There is a unitary asset register, but it is incomplete in certain respects and the link to long-term financing needs and service delivery is not strong.
indicators.advanced: There is a unitary and complete asset register linking to long-term financing needs and service delivery.

indicators.question: Asset data information system: Does the data information system meet short-term O&M requirements, by providing asset condition data, as well as enabling comprehensive and service-level performance analysis and optimization?
indicators.incipient: Any data information system, if there is one, does not provide useful asset condition data nor support service-level performance analysis.
indicators.nascent: The data information system partially serves short-term O&M requirements, by providing asset condition data, but does not enable service-level performance analysis.
indicators.emerging: The data information system partially serves short-term O&M requirements, by providing asset condition data, and enables some basic service-level performance analysis.
indicators.advanced: The data information system fully serves short-term O&M requirements, by providing asset condition data, and enables comprehensive and service-level performance analysis and optimization.

indicators.question: Asset accounting: Are accrual accounting principles, such as those outlined in IPSAS, applied to public asset management for better financial transparency and oversight?
indicators.incipient: Accrual accounting principles are not applied in relation to public asset management.
indicators.nascent: Accrual accounting principles are applied, but not in a systematic way in relation to public asset management.
indicators.emerging: Accrual accounting principles are applied to public asset management, but are not yet fully IPSAS compliant.
indicators.advanced: IPSAS-compliant accrual accounting principles are applied to public asset management for better financial transparency and oversight.

indicators.question: Formal audit and review: Is there a formal audit program for the public asset management system?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful audit program for the public asset management system.
indicators.nascent: Auditing of the public asset management system has been piloted or carried out on an ad hoc basis only and has involved only limited review and monitoring.
indicators.emerging: There is an audit program for the public asset management system, but some steps remain for it to be fully institutionalized, and review and monitoring are not yet systematic.
indicators.advanced: There is a formal audit program for the public asset management system, involving review and monitoring on a regular basis.

indicators.question: Annual performance review: Is there a formal process for carrying out annual performance reviews of the public asset management system?
indicators.incipient: There is no annual performance review of the public asset management system.
indicators.nascent: Performance reviews of the public asset management system have been piloted or carried out on an ad hoc basis only.
indicators.emerging: There is a process for carrying out performance reviews of the public asset management system, but some steps remain for it to be fully institutionalized.
indicators.advanced: There is a formalized process for carrying out annual performance reviews of the public asset management system on a regular basis.

indicators.question: PPP Policy: Is PPP policy well aligned with infrastructure development and PIM policies?
indicators.incipient: There is no PPP policy.
indicators.nascent: There is a PPP policy, but it is largely disconnected from infrastructure and PIM policies.
indicators.emerging: PPP policy is mostly aligned with infrastructure development and PIM policies, but there are no systematic connections between them.
indicators.advanced: PPP policy is fully aligned with infrastructure development and PIM policies.

indicators.question: Legal and regulatory framework for PPP: Is there an effective legal and regulatory framework for PPP, including an appropriate definition of PPP?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful legal and regulatory framework for PPP.
indicators.nascent: There is a basic legal framework for PPP, but the regulatory framework is largely undeveloped, or the definition of PPP is not consistent with international norms.
indicators.emerging: The legal framework for PPP is largely in place, including an appropriate definition of PPP, but there remain some important gaps in the details of the regulations.
indicators.advanced: PPP policy is fully aligned with infrastructure development and PIM policies.

indicators.question: PPP organization with technical expertise: Are the organizational arrangements for PPP, including a dedicated PPP unit, in place and working effectively, with adequate institutional capacity and technical expertise for assessing and managing PPP projects?
indicators.incipient: There are no organizational arrangements designed specifically for PPPs.
indicators.nascent: Organizational arrangements for PPP are in place, but there are some significant gaps in institutional capacity or technical expertise for assessing and managing PPP projects.
indicators.emerging: Organizational arrangements for PPP are in place, including a dedicated PPP unit, but there are some gaps in institutional capacity or technical expertise for assessing and managing PPP projects.
indicators.advanced: Effective organizational arrangements for PPP are in place, including a dedicated PPP unit, and there is adequate institutional capacity and technical expertise for assessing and managing PPP projects.

indicators.question: PPP appraisal: Is there a comprehensive appraisal process for PPPs, which conforms to the same process applied to traditionally implemented projects (TIPs) while extending to specialized areas of concern for PPPs and including independent review of appraisal quality and findings?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful appraisal process to determine if a PPP project will offer good public value.
indicators.nascent: There is an appraisal process for PPP projects, but it is largely detached from the process for TIPs and has no effective independent review.
indicators.emerging: There is an appraisal process for PPPs, which is mostly aligned with the process applied to TIPs, but it has no independent review step.
indicators.advanced: There is a comprehensive appraisal process for PPPs, which is fully aligned with the process applied to TIPs, while extending to all specialized areas of concern for PPPs, and which includes effective independent review of appraisal quality and findings.

indicators.question: Value for money assessment: Is there an assessment of value for money from adopting a PPP modality over traditional procurement, including possible use of a public sector comparator (PSC)?
indicators.incipient: There is no meaningful assessment of the value for money from adopting the PPP modality for a project.
indicators.nascent: There is a basic assessment of the value for money from adopting the PPP modality, but it is largely qualitative without a comparison with a PSC.
indicators.emerging: An assessment of value for money from adopting a PPP modality over traditional procurement is in place, which includes use of a PSC, but in limited areas/projects only.
indicators.advanced: An assessment of value for money from adopting a PPP modality over traditional procurement is in place, which includes full use of a PSC in all PPP areas/projects.

indicators.question: PPP selection criteria: Is value for money at the core of selection criteria for PPP projects?
indicators.incipient: PPP projects are selected using criteria other than value for money.
indicators.nascent: Value for money features as a concept in criteria for selecting PPP projects but no objective measure is specified.
indicators.emerging: Value for money is a criterion for selecting PPP projects.
indicators.advanced: Value for money is central to the selection criteria for PPP projects.
